source.title: METEOR: Evolutionary Journey of Large Language Models from Guidance to Self-Growth
source.authors: Jia-Wei Li; Xiao-An Xu; Yang Gao

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened or contain apparent transcription errors, but the weak-to-strong data-distillation tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: METEOR uses a weak-to-strong-inspired distillation step as part of its domain-evolution method, but it does not test whether the fine-tuned student beats the weak supervisor or report PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports quality scores for weak-guided distilled data and scores for models fine-tuned on that data, but neither result measures student performance against the weak supervisor or PGR. They are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. The paper's full-method results and its iterative-training and self-evolution results do not isolate the weak-to-strong distillation effect.
record.test_reason: METEOR borrows the weak-to-strong label only loosely. A weak model writes guidelines, GPT-4 (strong) writes answers, and the weak model is fine-tuned on them. That is ordinary strong-to-weak distillation with weak-written prompts, not a strong student trained on weak labels. No weak-supervisor baseline, strong ceiling or PGR is reported. Results compare guided with unguided distillation, and METEOR-trained with untrained models.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors claim each METEOR phase improves GPT-4-judged domain answers. They say guideline-based distillation aligns strong and weak knowledge distributions, but admit this is validated only indirectly. They also note the self-evolution gains are limited.
record.recipe_differences: The weak model generates guidelines for questions, GPT-4 generates answers following those guidelines, and the target model is fine-tuned on the resulting data. The study does not use the original student-versus-supervisor PGR evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported data-quality scores vary by category; scores for models fine-tuned on guided versus unguided distilled data also differ.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4 answers conditioned on weak-model guidelines scored about 9.07 versus 5.77 unguided on a GPT-4 data-quality score (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-model-written guidelines improve the GPT-4-judged quality of GPT-4-distilled domain data.

fits_no_version.finding: Weak models fine-tuned on guideline-conditioned GPT-4 data scored 9.04 (LLaMA3) and 9.22 (Qwen2), versus 5.38 and 6.13 for unguided data (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For 7-8B domain models, distillation data conditioned on the student's own guidelines yields better GPT-4-judged answers than unguided distillation.

record.problems: The weak-to-strong claim is not evaluated with a weak-supervisor baseline or PGR. The authors state that their distributional-difference hypothesis lacks direct experimental measurement. Reported evaluation uses GPT-4 as judge; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2, 5, and 6 are omitted because they report the integrated METEOR method or later iterative/self-evolution phases, not an isolated result for weak-to-strong distillation. They do not report a weak-supervisor comparison or PGR.

untested.parts: No strong student trained on weak labels and no PGR. The direction of supervision is strong to weak.
Guideline conditioning is not evaluated as a change in PGR.
No variation of supervisor or student size, task or representations against PGR.
No exploitation, distribution-shift or error-correlation tests.

record.verdict_notes: 'Weak-to-strong' here is a naming borrowed from Burns et al. In the paper, the weak model receives the strong model's outputs, so the paper bears on no version of the claim. All evaluation uses GPT-4 as judge, with no uncertainty reported. Table 2 has a corrupted cell ('c%').

versions.untested_parts: No direct comparison of a strong student with the weak supervisor, and no PGR.
Guidelines are compared with no guidelines, but the paper does not measure a change in PGR.
No PGR comparisons across supervisor or student sizes, tasks, or representations.
No tests of exploitability, distribution shift, or shared weak/strong errors.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.
No vision test of the claimed student-versus-supervisor effect.
